# Standalone Modkit editor

Modkit is a separate desktop application included with the game package. It
should feel like a small game editor: real game rendering, searchable resources,
direct manipulation, readable properties, useful errors and help beside the work.
The game launcher is for playing, settings and installing/enabling mod packages.
Android imports and manages mods; it does not expose creator tools.

## Architecture

Keep one runtime, package format and set of game-thread adapters. Separate
desktop entry points share the bundled Python/Qt runtime, rather than shipping
two copies or introducing a second project format. The editor has its own native
window, application identity and layout. It does not use the launcher's game
artwork, cartoon buttons or browser fallback as its interface.

Use Qt dock panels for projects/files, a source workspace, the live viewport,
assets, properties, output and help. Panels can be rearranged or hidden. Restore
a useful layout from the View menu. Keyboard shortcuts, visible dirty state,
source revision checks and clear Test/Stop/Export actions are required.

The viewport hosts only the editor's own Test process on supported Windows/X11
systems. It displays the real native renderer and receives normal game input.
When embedding is unavailable, open the same game in its own window and explain
the platform limitation. Do not substitute a screenshot or pretend preview.

The existing authenticated creator bridge is the live connection. Keep requests
bounded, asynchronous and bound to the selected project and exact Test process.
Reuse native Scene/Mission pages and ownership rules for edits. No arbitrary
memory writes, stale native handles or second spawning implementation.

## Delivery stages

1. **Separate applications.** Ship Windows/Linux Modkit entry points, professional
   native project/source/property panels, built-in reference and guides, and the
   existing create/edit/validate/Test/apply/export workflow. Remove authoring from
   the desktop game launcher and Android. Preserve existing projects and progress.
2. **Live scene workspace.** Embed the owned Test renderer, browse current native
   assets, drag supported props into the scene, select owned objects and edit
   transforms through the same Scene editor operations. Save portable drafts,
   apply, export and load the package in another session. Explain placement and
   supported classes honestly; a factory call alone does not qualify an NPC.
3. **Whole-library authoring.** Add indexed unloaded resources, dependency and
   memory-cost feedback, source preparation/cancellation, source-aware previews
   and typed import/export. Native loader, collision and lifecycle checks gate
   each asset family. Keep large scans off the UI/game threads.
4. **Direct manipulation.** Add camera-correct picking, move/rotate/scale gizmos,
   snapping, selection outlines, multi-selection and bounded transactions. Picking
   must use proven matrices/hits; a guessed mouse-to-world projection is not a
   finished placement tool. Retain the same undo/document/ownership contracts.
5. **Mission and cinematic workspaces.** Build visual objectives, encounters and
   camera tracks on the public services. Add campaign/HUD integration only after
   proving its native lifecycle. Keep videos and simulation timing correct.
6. **Creator experience.** Add guided first projects, contextual examples, an
   offline searchable API/help system, readable diagnostics, localization tools,
   asset validation and complete acceptance projects. Explain prerequisites and
   unsupported edits before users lose work.

Stages may overlap, but qualify complete workflows. Record implemented behavior,
actual platform evidence and remaining work in coverage.json and the work log.
Do not advertise the full kit as released until the full gate in PLAN.md passes.

## Workspace update

The desktop workspace now keeps separate source tabs, unsaved buffers and undo
histories, with revision-checked Save All and explicit conflict recovery. Find
and replace, Quick open, a command palette and contextual offline help support
keyboard authoring. Assets use a filtered model with categories and portable
favorites. The searchable scene outliner and Inspector edit both the native live
scene and validated saved source objects; offline changes use source undo and
preserve complete basis vectors. Background reads do not drop foreground edits.

The expanded Qt workflow and creator Python checks cover source retention,
partial save failure, portable favorites, offline transforms and undo, read-only
Test sources and world-change handle refresh. A private Linux X11 run separately
qualifies real renderer embedding, loaded prop placement, native transform
changes, undo/redo, draft application and credited disabled package import.
Native Windows drivers, viewport picking, gizmos, collision authoring and the
remaining full release gate need separate qualification. Cross-level prop
previews are covered by the later viewport workflows below.

## Viewport preview workflows

Direct level previews read the player's installed gameflow through the same
parser used by checkpoint sweeps. Standard map entries retain their original
configuration. The editor mounts only a private gameflow override over the
original archives, starts with fresh Test progress and drives the original
menus. Paused/free native camera modes, explicit framing distance and balanced
actor-visibility leases keep authoring independent of campaign progression.
The whole-library browser uses bounded native queries, source preparation,
cancel/status services and temporary owned prop previews. Preview objects do
not enter Scene documents or get silently exported.

Private Linux runs qualify automatic Land of Chocolate and Bartman Begins
entry, paused camera/framing, geometry and selection filters, balanced reveal,
and a Land of Chocolate prop loaded/rendered/removed in Bartman Begins. Both
runs retain native Scene placement/edit/undo/draft/export behavior. Other
platform execution and the rest of the campaign remain separate evidence.

Next delivery order:

1. Dedicated previews for textures/materials, audio and animation, with source
   identity and supported-format diagnostics. General resources must not be
   mislabeled as spawnable props.
2. A native studio/world visibility path for isolated asset backgrounds and
   reviewed camera bounds, followed by camera-correct picking and gizmos.
3. Full base-world outliner, category visibility and live checkpoint navigation,
   with lifecycle, collision and original-save qualification per asset family.
4. Finish the mission, encounter, cinematic and package acceptance projects in
   PLAN.md; retain the independent Windows/Linux creator and Android consumer
   boundary. A source compile is not native-driver/device acceptance.

Offline geometry preview now has a separate read-only asset path using the
existing native format readers. Indexing/decoding run off the UI thread, source
identities are checked, and a bounded cache feeds real vertex/index buffers to
rotating hover cards and an interactive inspection view. A private Linux GPU
run indexes 19,994 resources without launching gameplay, then renders and orbits
the original 363-vertex, 498-triangle coffee-table resource. These neutral,
bind-pose mesh views do not replace native material/behavior qualification or
complete offline world authoring and transform gizmos.

## Acceptance

- Launch the game launcher and Modkit independently and together; they must not
  start duplicate games, corrupt source files, alter normal saves during Test or
  compete for one local server/window identity.
- Create a credited project, edit/save Lua and guided mission properties, reject
  stale source edits, validate, Test, apply actual saved drafts, export and import
  disabled. Close with unsaved changes without silently discarding them.
- Observe real renderer frames in the viewport, use native menu/game input,
  place a supported prop from the asset panel, change its pose, undo/redo and
  remove it. Saved documents and original game resources must remain correct.
- Provide useful empty, loading, disconnected, missing-runtime and failed-import
  states. Every visible action works or explains its exact prerequisite.
- Check Windows and Linux packaging, keyboard navigation and Steam Deck screen
  sizes. Compilation and native-driver/device execution are separate evidence.
- Maintain the Steam Deck's 25 GiB disk reserve; share runtime artifacts and build
  incrementally. Never publish game data or overwrite user projects and saves.

# Getting started with Modkit

Open **The Simpsons Game Modkit** from the desktop application menu or the
separate Modkit entry in the game package. The game launcher also has an
**Open Modkit** shortcut in Mods. Android imports and manages mod ZIPs;
authoring takes place in the desktop application.

## Your first project

1. Choose **File → New project**. Start with **Scene editor** to place props,
   **Mission editor** for route objectives and props, or another commented
   template for gameplay, combat or camera work.
2. Enter a name, stable id and creator credit. A project starts disabled and
   does not change your ordinary game profile.
3. Use **Project files** or **Ctrl+P** to open Lua, README or mod.json. Each file
   keeps its own tab, cursor, undo history and unsaved changes. **Ctrl+S** saves
   the current file; **Ctrl+Shift+S** saves all changed files. An asterisk marks
   unsaved work. Closing a changed file or switching projects offers Save,
   Discard and Cancel. A conflicting external edit is rejected before overwriting.
4. Choose **Validate** to check files, dependencies and package metadata.
   Validation is separate from proving behavior in the game.
5. Choose **Test** or press **F5**. The viewport hosts the real game on Windows
   and Linux X11. Test uses this project's separate progress and leaves normal
   saves alone. Alternatively, choose a map above the viewport and **Load level**
   to go directly into a fresh private preview with a paused camera.

Validate, Test and Export save changed source files first. If any save fails,
the requested action stops and the affected buffer remains open. Earlier files
that saved successfully keep their new revisions. **File → Reload file from
disk** rereads an externally edited file after the usual unsaved-change check;
it does not silently overwrite your editor buffer.

**Ctrl+F** finds text; **Ctrl+H** opens replacement tools. Search supports case,
whole words and wraparound. Replace All is one undoable edit and cannot modify
read-only files during Test. **Ctrl+G** goes to a source line. New lines retain
the current indentation. Script failures open Output and include recent per-mod
file/line diagnostics from the game log when available.

## Scene workspace

The viewport's level picker reads the original gameflow from your installed
files, including a project's gameflow replacement when present. **Load level**
selects one standard-mode map entry, keeping its original player overrides,
checkpoint and extension flags. The game operates its own starting menus;
you do not need to play through earlier episodes. Each direct preview has
fresh private progress and a one-file gameflow override. Normal game files,
the launcher's selected start episode and your saves are kept intact. Ordinary
**Test / F5** still opens the project's persistent Test progress.

Use **Paused editor** to freeze simulation and fly the native camera; **Free
camera** leaves simulation running. Click the viewport for WASD movement,
arrow-key look, Q/E height, Shift/Ctrl speed and 1/3 zoom. **Frame selection**
positions the camera toward the live outliner selection; the distance field
also controls temporary preview framing for large or small props.

**Map geometry** hides supported factory actors, leaving the static world.
**Isolate selected actor** keeps one live authored actor visible against the
world. **Full scene** releases only the editor's hide requests, preserving
the game's scripted visibility. These are preview filters; they do not delete
entities, remove collision, rewrite archives or export with your mod. Other
entity layouts and effects can remain visible and are reported in the status.
Filters reset on world changes and when an isolated actor is removed.

Once a level is ready, **Assets** lists loaded native resources. Search by name,
class, archive or GUID; multiple words narrow the results together. Category
and **Placeable props** filters help separate supported props from other resource
types. Right-click a resource to bookmark it or copy its source identity.
**Favorites** persist across Test sessions using source GUIDs and archive paths,
rather than temporary game handles. Select an asset for its type, archive and
definition details in Inspector. Supported props can be dragged into the viewport or
double-clicked. The current placement rule puts the prop beside your controlled
character. It does not guess a collision hit underneath the mouse pointer.

Current Scene projects select exact live template identities. Repeated placement
reuses the loaded choices instead of rebuilding the whole catalog on every click;
an out-of-date catalog is refreshed before selection. Older projects with numbered
template choices remain compatible. Runtime handles stay local to the preview,
and saved scenes retain portable GUIDs and source paths. Script safety budgets
remain unchanged.

**Scene outliner** lists authored objects with searchable names, tags and source
types. Select one to inspect its position, source and identity. **Inspector**
exposes XYZ, rotation, scale, duplication and removal. During Test, Scene undo/redo
uses the same history as the native in-game editor. These operations preserve
the same stable object tags, source
retention and save documents; the desktop application does not spawn unrelated
copies through a separate factory.

Outside Test, opening mod.json also exposes saved scene objects in the outliner.
Rename, reposition, rotate, resize, duplicate or remove them without launching
the game. These changes edit the validated portable scene in mod.json and use
its source undo history; they preserve all three basis vectors, including
nonuniform scale. **Alt+Z** and **Alt+Shift+Z** undo and redo scene edits in either
mode. Save All keeps offline edits; Test loads them through the existing scene
service. Offline authoring does not render or check collision. Names are edited
outside Test; live placement and transforms still use native services.

The **Whole game** asset tab searches the native archive index with categories
and paging, including outside Test. Hover a model for a rotating geometry card,
or open **3D preview** to orbit, pan, zoom and frame its real decoded mesh. See
[Asset previews](ASSET_PREVIEWS.md) for format support and extension points.
Select a resource for its source details, then **Prepare source**
to retain its original archive and dependencies. If a resource has multiple
definitions, the source picker pages through all of them rather than silently
truncating its variants. Source loading reports native progress and supports
cancellation. **Native prop preview** creates a temporary native prop in front of the
camera, frames it and isolates it from supported actors. **Clear preview**
removes only that temporary object; it never writes it into your scene document.
To author a lasting object, find the prepared prop under **Loaded resources**
and place it through the Scene editor. Save live drafts to keep that placement.

The browser can inspect models, textures, audio and other resources. Native
prop preview qualifies prop factories; it does not activate arbitrary NPC AI or
pretend that every indexed resource is an entity. Dedicated material/texture,
audio and animation preview surfaces, collision-rich placement, picking and
gizmos remain in the implementation plan.

Open **Options → Extras → Mods** in Test for the project's native Scene,
Mission, Camera or Combat editor. This includes mission point placement,
prerequisites, preview start/failure/retry and camera controls. The desktop
Inspector also edits mission names, rules and prerequisites when mod.json is
open outside Test.

## Keep and share your work

Choose **Save live drafts**, wait for confirmation, then stop Test. **Apply
saved drafts** checks their source fingerprint and updates the project's
mod.json. Mission and scene documents are applied together. Save any source
changes before starting another Test or exporting.

Draft application follows the most recently launched Test, including direct
level previews. Switching levels restarts Test and asks before discarding
unsaved live edits. Save and apply drafts before switching to keep them. Source
files keep their normal revision and unsaved-buffer protection throughout.

Choose **Export package** and a destination ZIP. Creator credit, requirements
and checksums travel with it. A player imports the ZIP in the game launcher's
Mods tab or the Android app, then enables it. Imported mods start disabled.

## Find help and arrange the workspace

**F1** opens the matching API reference when the source cursor is on a game
operation; elsewhere it opens Getting started. Help search covers guide text,
API descriptions and parameter names. Search named operations such as
world.spawn, entities.set_transform or missions.advance_batch. Read the
parameters and ownership rules before extending a template. Source comments
address modders and use public operations instead of generated addresses.

Use **View** to show or hide panels; drag dock headers to rearrange them.
Narrow or tiled windows automatically group the side panels into one tabbed
column, leaving room for the viewport and source. **View → Compact workspace**
also selects this layout manually. Wider windows restore the previous layout;
Reset workspace layout returns to automatic sizing.
**Ctrl+Shift+P** opens a searchable command palette for available actions,
project files and guides. Unavailable actions stay disabled. The toolbar keeps
the common Create, Save All, Validate, Test, Stop and Export actions together;
draft actions remain in the File and Project menus.
**Reset workspace layout** restores the starting arrangement. Output keeps
validation messages and actionable errors. Source editing and project switching
wait until Test closes; live scene edits go through the native creator bridge.
Files may be read during Test but cannot be edited. Background polling keeps
an active Inspector field intact; a foreground edit waits for a poll to finish
instead of disappearing behind it.

The viewport only embeds the editor's own Test process. Linux Wayland display
servers that do not expose foreign windows use the real game in its own window;
asset/property editing still uses the same authenticated session. There is no
screenshot-based renderer or separate rendering implementation.

# Objects, source loading and ownership

Mods create an object with `game.world.spawn(template.id, position, radius)` using
a resident template from `game.world.catalog()`. The return value is a temporary
handle. The host records its mod and runtime generation; guest addresses are not
public object identities.

Catalog records include the original `class` and `model_resource`, a native
resource GUID for supported models. Different model resources stay separate
even when their display labels match. An empty model ID means that layout has
no reviewed identity adapter. A class or shared model does not establish every
scripted behavior, costume override or collision dependency. Distinct native
definitions remain separate even when both the class and model agree.

The catalog also includes reviewed placeable definitions retained by a fully
loaded source stream. These can have `seen = 0`: no live source object is
required. Their handles retain the original definition GUID, stream-load key
and world generation. Destroying a source instance need not expire its
definition; unloading or reloading its source stream does. Source data stays
owned by the original loader, and clones join that source's native teardown
list. Plain catalog queries do not request archives or start another level.

The debug menu's **Game-wide library** links named models, character banks and
mesh parts to the original object definitions that use them. Names come from
compiled property groups and model metadata before an instance is spawned.
Artist names get readable spacing and known aliases; the original resource name
and source path remain visible. Different original behavior variants stay separate.
Open an object and choose **Load and spawn** to load its source and spawn it in
front of your character. The operation continues with the menu closed. Textures,
audio and other standalone resources are still resources, rather than entities.

The debug menu's **Spawner → Objects from other levels** browser can retain up
to eight additional native archives and their dependencies. Sources are grouped
by episode for browsing. Their actors stay inactive while the host retains their
definitions for the regular spawner and `world.catalog()`. Loading another source
keeps earlier objects. Additions are serialized; a failed or canceled addition
retires only its new files and protects the accepted session and current level.
Close the menu to keep a source loaded. **Cancel source load** preserves earlier
sources and copies; **Remove sources and their objects** releases the menu's
lease and removes its copies. Other owners keep their objects and shared files.

Mods use the same path through `assets.templates`, `assets.load_source`,
`assets.source_status`, `assets.source_streams` and `assets.release_source`.
Each generation leases the whole session; `source_status().stream` identifies
its latest requested root, while `source_streams()` lists all accepted roots.
Native archives can share dependencies, so accepted archives stay together
until the last owner releases the session. A new request reports `busy` while
another addition is in progress and `resource_limit` after eight roots.
`assets.cancel_source()` withdraws the caller's pending request, restoring its
earlier lease. With multiple requesters, another owner's request can continue.
Require `assets.source_streams` in a manifest that depends on these semantics;
older single-source hosts do not expose that operation.

A successful `world.spawn` from a retained source automatically acquires a lease
for the spawning mod, even if another mod originally loaded it. Removing the
loader mod preserves the new owner's copy and resources. An already loaded
dependency joins its original source without another native stream load.
Failed additions restore previous claims, including a lease acquired by spawning
from an accepted source during preparation. Objects cannot be created from new
files until the addition commits or from a session being retired.

Reload transfers supported claims and objects. Exact saves retain all archive
paths, per-file ownership and native load identities alongside guest memory;
preflight checks every claim before replacing that memory. Legacy single-source
exact saves remain readable. Checkpoint loads start their own level normally.
Wait for additions, cancellations and releases to finish before an exact save.
Cleanup checks each file's load key, address and name and protects other current
level files, including files streamed after the session began.

The [Library objects example](examples/library-objects/main.lua) contains comments
for modders and an original in-game Options page. Create it from Modkit's
creator tools, or with `modkit.py new "Library objects" --template library-objects`. It never
spawns automatically: inspect, choose an original variant, load, then spawn.
Reacquire `resident_template` after loading or restoring; an asset ID or source
GUID is metadata, not a temporary entity template handle.

This cross-level path is experimental. Loading a resource does not establish
the scene setup a boss, scripted encounter or other specialized class needs.
The Linux qualification combines eight archives and three independently posed
ScriptableProps, including shared-resource preservation, native-IO cancellation,
exact save/restore, code reload and last-owner retirement.
Native Windows and Pixel behavior remain separate acceptance work.

The native class registry supplies class names and sizes. Existing registered
objects with a native frame can establish additional placeable classes;
non-world factory services are excluded. The debug spawner shows additional
categories automatically. Broader class-specific physics, AI and script behavior
still require acceptance checks; a factory registration alone is not that proof.

Use `game.assets.search(nil, nil, 0, 20, template.model_resource)` to find the
model's named source metadata. Asset locations include `resource_id`; native
IDs contain 32 hexadecimal digits and are separate from temporary entity or
asset handles. This asynchronous library search does not load a model into
the level. Catalog labels normally come from the game's own named-resource
load, with matching library metadata available after its scan. Plain
`world.catalog()` calls never start a whole-game disk scan. Names are owned
strings tied to the current native payload; ambiguous IDs do not supply a
guessed label. See the [native model notes](../simpsons/re/entity_assets.md).

The [Combat workshop](COMBAT.md#combat-workshop) includes a native-menu template
picker. It keeps the selected resource across label changes and code reload,
and preserves the encounter's model separately from a template being browsed.
If a checkpoint's model is no longer loaded, retry fails without substitution.

`game.world.owned()` lists this generation's live objects as `{id, class}` records.
`game.world.destroy(id)` queues removal, returning true for its first request and
false for another request before cleanup. A foreign owner receives `not_owner`;
an expired identity receives `stale_handle`. Players, stock level entities and
another mod's objects cannot be removed through this operation.

```lua
-- Choose a suitable loaded prop, rather than an unloaded assets.search result.
local actor = game.players.controlled(0)
if actor then
    local p = actor.position
    game.world.spawn(template.id, {x = p.x + 4, y = p.y + 1, z = p.z}, 1)
end
for _, object in ipairs(game.world.owned()) do
    game.world.destroy(object.id)
end
```

## Transforms

`game.entities.transform(id)` reads an owned object's current world-space
`position`, `right`, `up` and `forward` vectors. The basis includes scale and may
be sheared; it is not a set of angles. The original RenderWare getter resolves
pending frame and parent updates before returning the transform.

`game.entities.move(id, position)` changes world position through the class's
original setter. This preserves the basis and includes the class's controller
and model notifications. Rotated, scaled and sheared parents are converted to
local coordinates first. Invalid frames and singular parents fail with
`unsupported` before calling the setter. Placement never scans memory for
coordinates or rewrites unrelated fields that happen to contain similar values.

`game.entities.set_transform(id, transform)` changes the complete world-space
pose: position and all three basis vectors. The original class matrix setter
updates its cached scale, queues the frame update and notifies its model;
character overrides also receive their controller update. All four vectors are
converted through the parent before dispatch. Zero or dependent axes, nonfinite
values and scales outside the original float32 length calculation's range fail
before the setter. Unsupported frames, singular parents and missing setters
have no direct-memory fallback.

```lua
-- Read a current identity from world.owned(), rather than keeping a saved ID.
local objects = game.world.owned()
if objects[1] then
    local object = objects[1].id
    local transform = game.entities.transform(object)
    local p = transform.position
    game.entities.move(object, {x = p.x + 2, y = p.y, z = p.z})
end
```

```lua
-- Make my first object 10% larger while keeping its current world position.
local objects = game.world.owned()
if objects[1] then
    local id = objects[1].id
    local pose = game.entities.transform(id)
    for _, name in ipairs({"right", "up", "forward"}) do
        local v = pose[name]
        pose[name] = {x = v.x * 1.1, y = v.y * 1.1, z = v.z * 1.1}
    end
    game.entities.set_transform(id, pose)
end
```

The commented **Owned objects** creator project adds native menu actions to
move, rotate around world Y, grow and shrink the latest owned prop. Clear also
releases a source automatically retained by a cross-level spawn. C++ plugins
use `Game::Transform`, `Game::Move` and `Game::SetTransform` with the same rules.

These operations reject another mod's owner, an older runtime generation and
objects whose removal is already queued. They are placement operations: they
do not sweep for collision clearance or disable an object's scripted movement.
Author safe destinations and class behavior. Arbitrary shape, rig and collision
imports remain separate authoring work.
Player teleports and the debug camera's family placement use the same class
dispatch, including the character controller's original placement call.

For a template that may reject cloning, use
`game.system.try_call("world.spawn", {template = template.id, position = p})`.
Its reply contains `ok` and either `value` or `code`/`error`. It handles one named
host operation while retaining argument, ownership and lifecycle restrictions.
Lua `pcall` is unavailable in this bounded sandbox; callback errors and exhausted
budgets still retire the mod. The commented creator example shows both spawn
and transform failure handling without protecting arbitrary script functions.

The limits are 64 objects per owner and 1,024 per profile, checked before calling
the factory. Pending removal still counts until destruction completes, but is
excluded from live queries and saved ownership so reload cannot bring it back.

## Visibility and encounter setup

`game.entities.render_state(id)` reports `hidden_by_mod`, `hide_count`,
`has_model` and `scene_attached`. An unsupported native layout returns `nil`.
Scene attachment means the object belongs to the renderer's spatial scene;
camera culling, occlusion, model resources and authored behavior still determine
what is drawn. A template's class label is not a costume or faction guarantee.

`game.entities.set_visible(id, false)` adds one native hide request for this
owner. Calling it again does not add another. `set_visible(id, true)` releases
that request, preserving other native hide requests. It does not force an
authored hidden object to appear. The native scene/model callbacks perform
attachment and removal; mods do not edit render flags or draw over the game.

```lua
local object = game.world.owned()[1]
if object then
    local state = game.entities.render_state(object.id)
    if state then
        game.entities.set_visible(object.id, state.hidden_by_mod)
    end
end
```

The request transfers on code reload and exact ownership restore without
incrementing the native counter again. A native force-show cancels it, so a
later mod reveal cannot consume a newer authored hide request. Checkpoints
create a fresh world; recreate the desired state with the new objects. Unknown
layouts reject a visibility change with `unsupported`; a full native counter
rejects with `resource_limit`. A callback that removes the object returns `nil`.

Visibility leaves AI, collision, damage and audio running. Use it for staging
or visual changes; it does not suspend enemies or establish an encounter's
navigation and behavior. Combat workshop includes native menu actions to hide
and reveal its own targets.

## Removal and lifecycle

The [combat guide](COMBAT.md) covers typed owned health, native damage/healing
and `entity.died`. Ordinary removal does not establish a defeat. These services
share the lifetime and ownership rules below.

Cleanup runs on the game thread after callbacks return. The original helper
chooses the class deleting destructor or subscriber destruction path, allowing
normal physics, component, subscription and world-list cleanup. Each request is
claimed once. A class that completes later remains tracked without receiving
another destruction request. Batches stop at 16 requests or approximately 2 ms,
apart from the request already in progress.

A callback fault retires that mod's objects; dependents retire on their next
dispatch. Unrelated owners remain active. Shutdown on a worker queues host state
only, without calling stopped guest threads. The game owns final world teardown.

The owner receives `entity.removed` after a gameplay deletion or completed
`world.destroy`. It carries `entity` (now stale) and `reason` (`game` or `removed`).
Notifications do not cross runtime generations. Use `level.unloading` for whole
world teardown; it does not replay individual removal events.

The base destructor invalidates a lifetime before memory is freed. Reusing the
same address, GUID and class still produces a new identity. Player, entity and
template handles reject reuse before reading the old allocation. Spawned copies
do not replace their source templates in the catalog.

## Reload and saves

Reload transfers live objects without a despawn/respawn cycle. Preparation acquires
nothing. Once the old runtime retires, the replacement adopts its own matching
objects before cleanup drains. Discarding failed preparation cannot release a live
owner. Requery `world.owned()` in `code.reloaded`; earlier handles have expired.

A checkpoint starts a new world. Its old objects cannot be adopted into that world
or destroyed through stale pointers. An authored mission must recreate intended
objects from its saved mission data and supported loaded templates. Do not save
object handles in `game.state`.

Exact-snapshot ownership records contain GUIDs, class names and type signatures,
without guest addresses. Commit drops old host identities and resolves reserved
mod GUIDs in the restored direct entity index, adopting restored allocations
instead of making copies. Isolated ownership and original-routine fixtures cover
this contract; full in-game exact-snapshot qualification remains required.
The loaded-template catalog is invalidated on rewind. Reconstructing it from
snapshot metadata is still required for complete spawn authoring after restore.

## Creator project and boundaries

Choose **Owned objects** in desktop or Android **File → New project** in Modkit. Its commented
Lua project uses **Options → Extras → Mods** to select loaded props, spawn beside
the character using the page, move its latest object and remove its own objects.
Projects start disabled.
This development example uses the public object-ownership APIs and starts disabled.

The factory and world registration are separate loader steps. Clones receive a
unique GUID before registration, enter the direct entity index and join the source
layer's normal teardown list. They do not borrow or modify streaming GUID nodes.
An initializer that already registered its new instance is detached through the
original unregister routine before unique registration. A factory returning its
existing source instance rejects cloning without destroying that source.

This does not load cross-level dependencies or prove every class safe to duplicate.
Encounters, collectibles and scripted objects may need class-specific setup.
Rotation/scale editing, general component/lifecycle queries and cross-level
streaming remain in the full kit plan. Native Windows and Pixel runs are
qualified separately from compilation and Proton fixtures.

The private Linux GAME_HUB check covers ScriptableProp placement and movement,
unchanged basis and source templates, independent owners, menu actions, player
teleport, reload and retirement with a clean exit. The sampled prop has no bodies
in its owned Havok body list; collision-rich classes need their own acceptance
checks. The original-routine fixture separately covers affine and nested parents,
controller dispatch, invalid hierarchies and singular transforms. These checks
do not qualify arbitrary class physics, scripted behavior or the whole campaign.

# Your first mod

Open the separate **Modkit** desktop application and choose **File → New project**.
Enter your name for the creator credit. Projects start disabled; **Test** uses
separate progress and leaves your normal saves alone.

| Start with | What you can change |
| --- | --- |
| Script starter | A small native Options page, an action and a saved counter. |
| Player actions | An ability for the character controlled by P1 or P2, with independent cooldowns. |
| Timed events | A delayed gameplay action that pauses with the game and survives supported mod-state restores. |
| Scene editor | Supported native props, placement, transforms and saved scene drafts. |
| There and back | Mission objectives, failure, retry points and saved progress. |
| File replacements | Your edited files at their original relative paths beneath `gamedata/`. |

For a first project, choose **Script starter**. Open `locales/en.json` and change
the page title and action label. Open `main.lua`: its comments explain where to
put your action and why saved values belong in `game.state`.

Use **Validate**, then **Test**. In the game, open **Options → Extras → Mods**
and select your page. Use the code reload action for Lua-only edits. Resource,
metadata and translation changes need a restart of Test.

Use **Export package** to create a ZIP with your name, version and checksums.
Other players import it from the launcher's **Mods** tab. Android imports and
manages these packages; authoring stays in the desktop Modkit.

Keep display words in `locales/en.json` and stable keys in Lua. This lets others
[translate your mod](TRANSLATIONS.md) without changing its behavior. Read the
built-in API reference before adding a named operation; unsupported asset
types or behaviors still need a reviewed native adapter.

Do not distribute `default.xex`, unmodified game archives or someone else's
game files with your project. Small language packs contain translated strings,
and data packages should contain only your own supported replacements.
guides.MESHES.md:
# Mesh attribute editing

The mesh tools export supported preinstanced geometry to OBJ and build edited
positions, normals and UVs into a small, source-checked mod. The native loader applies the
edit before it creates the original rendering resources. The game keeps ownership
of the model, materials, buffers and teardown.

The writer preserves vertex counts, order, triangulated topology and materials.
Normals and UVs stay unchanged unless their import is selected. Edited static
positions must stay inside the original box and sphere. Reviewed skinned streams
support UV-only edits, with positions, normals and weights kept intact.
Unreviewed declarations and multipart native sections remain read-only.
New topology, imported characters, automatic normal generation,
rigs, animation and collision are separate work in the [full kit](PLAN.md).

## Inspect your source

Build the standalone tool without rebuilding the game:

```sh
cmake -S modkit -B /path/to/modkit-build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build /path/to/modkit-build -j2 --target modkit_streams
```

Find a mesh in the asset library or a deep stream index. Use its exact resource
GUID when multiple resources share a name. For example, this reads the coffee
table from your own installed files:

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py --gamedata /path/to/gamedata mesh inspect gamehub/gamehub/zone13.str 6 9D47543EE15FF766E15FF766E15FF766 /path/to/table.json --stream-tool /path/to/modkit-build/modkit_streams
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py mesh export /path/to/table.json /path/to/table.obj
```

The JSON records position `editable`, `normals_editable` and `uvs_editable`
capabilities with their reasons. It also records
the resource identity, exact source hash, original positions, triangle indices
and bounds. Keep those inspection fields intact. The native vertex count can
differ from the old source count because preinstancing can split or compact
vertices; the OBJ uses the allocation the renderer actually draws.

## Edit and package

Edit the OBJ's positions in your modeling tool. Preserve `geometry_0` and other
exported object names, vertex order, face winding and triangles. Disable vertex
welding, reordering and coordinate conversion on import/export. UV and normal
records are imported only when requested. Export a triangulated OBJ.

A small uniform shrink around the original sphere center is the qualified
starting example. Position-only deformation still uses the original normals and
collision. Use the normal workflow below when the shape needs new lighting directions;
physical interaction keeps its original collision.
The writer rejects positions outside the original culling bounds.

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py mesh import /path/to/table.json /path/to/edited-table.obj /path/to/edited-table.json
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py new "My table" --kind data --id yourname.table --author "Your name"
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py --gamedata /path/to/gamedata mesh build yourname.table /path/to/edited-table.json --stream-tool /path/to/modkit-build/modkit_streams
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py validate yourname.table
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py pack yourname.table
```

`mesh build` verifies the source, geometry layout and complete edit before
updating `assets/mesh-edits.json` and the manifest's `mesh_edits` path. Building
another resource adds it to the same catalog; rebuilding an identity replaces
its previous edit. The package stores compact attribute edits and fingerprints,
without copying a game archive or DFF. Keep your full inspection JSON and OBJ
separately for further editing. Re-exporting an edited document includes its
current changes. `--geometry geometry:N` exports a supported subset; importing
that subset preserves pending edits to other geometries.

Test through the [isolated creator workflow](CREATOR_WORKFLOW.md), then import
the ZIP through Mods. Imported packages keep their creator credit and remain
disabled until enabled. Restart the game after changing mesh assets. Code reload
reports that a restart is required and retains the active prepared selection.

## Import matching normals

Inspect `normals_editable` and `normals_reason` for each geometry. The reviewed
static stream can be included in OBJ with `--normals`:

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py mesh export /path/to/table.json /path/to/table-with-normals.obj --normals
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py mesh import /path/to/table.json /path/to/edited-table-with-normals.obj /path/to/edited-table.json --normals
```

Edit or recalculate normals in your modeling tool, then export face-corner
normal references. Keep the original vertex splits: one preserved vertex cannot
have different normals on different faces. The importer rejects that conflict
instead of choosing one direction. Unreferenced vertices retain their previous
normals, and position-only reimports preserve pending normal edits.

Normals must be finite unit vectors; the validator allows the original packed
stream's quantization tolerance. The native writer stores signed ten-bit XYZ,
preserving the fourth component and every unrelated byte. An unchanged OBJ
normal round-trip preserves the complete original coffee-table resource exactly.
Earlier position-only inspection documents still work; inspect again to obtain
the added normal metadata before using `--normals`.

## Edit texture coordinates

Use `--uvs` to export and import the reviewed primary texture-coordinate stream.
For example, Frink's first geometry supports UV editing while its skinned
positions stay read-only:

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py --gamedata /path/to/gamedata mesh inspect gamehub/gamehub.str 19 2C04E125EA57CADCEA57CADCEA57CADC /path/to/frink.json --stream-tool /path/to/modkit-build/modkit_streams
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py mesh export /path/to/frink.json /path/to/frink.obj --uvs --geometry geometry:0
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py mesh import /path/to/frink.json /path/to/edited-frink.obj /path/to/edited-frink.json --uvs
```

Build and package that document with the same `mesh build` workflow above.
Export selects geometries supporting the requested streams; `--geometry` chooses
a specific subset. `--normals --uvs` includes both where both are supported.

UVs use the game's original U/V orientation, without an implicit image flip or
0–1 clamp. Negative coordinates and repeats are preserved. The importer requires
two finite float32 components and preserves the original UV seams. Different
face-corner UVs cannot be assigned to one preserved vertex; that needs a topology
edit, which this writer does not perform.

On UV-only geometry, changing a preview vertex position is rejected. Unchanged
positions are omitted from normal/UV import documents, and unreferenced vertices
keep their prior attributes. Reimporting one stream preserves pending changes to
the other streams. Earlier inspection documents remain compatible; inspect again
to obtain UV capability metadata. This edits texture mapping, with the existing
textures, materials and rig retained. Texture-image and rig import are separate.

## Validation and priority

The first requested mod wins a whole resource; dependencies have lower priority.
Conflicts appear as `mesh:<resource-id>`. Edits to the same GUID are not silently
combined. A source mismatch leaves the resource unchanged and identifies the
mod in the log.

Catalogs are verified and captured before play. Each mod supports up to 64 mesh
resources in a 16 MiB catalog; a profile supports up to 1,024 entries and 64 MiB
of prepared catalogs. The loader checks the exact named-resource fingerprint,
supported geometry and requested attributes before copying same-size
bytes into the game-owned input. It then follows the original load path. The callback does not
read package files or allocate replacement GPU resources.

For an extracted named chunk, `modkit_streams mesh-inspect RESOURCE [OUTPUT]`
describes it and `mesh-edit RESOURCE DOCUMENT OUTPUT` writes an edited copy.
These outputs require new paths. The artist-facing commands above select the
resource directly from the installed STR and preserve its source location.

## Qualification

The original relocation and copy/rebase routines agree with the host reader on
all 5,533 mesh resources and 20,490 native blocks in the private installed-game
inventory, with no failures. The reader identifies 3,145 static geometries within
the first writer's supported layouts. That is format coverage, rather than a
claim that every geometry has been edited and played through.

The normal codec also round-trips 1,881,360 packed normals across 2,825 supported
static geometries without changing any bits. Native field literals, alternate
negative-one encoding, the preserved fourth component and malformed directions
have focused fixture checks.

The UV writer also preserves all bytes in no-op edits across 3,313 resources:
15,321 geometries and 6,436,832 UV pairs, including 12,176 skinned geometries.
Position and normal coverage remains unchanged. A private Linux Vulkan Frink
edit verifies all 36,624 bytes of the bound vertex stream: only the requested
UV bytes differ, with skinning, positions, normals and other attributes intact.
The owned NPC renders from both sides, retains the stream through simulation,
removes with world count restored and exits cleanly with the audio pause fix.

A private Linux Vulkan test loads edited pickup and coffee-table resources. It
compares all 363 coffee-table vertices with the imported edit, renders front and
back views of an owned prop using that geometry, removes it and restores the
original world count before exiting cleanly. A second run changes the table's
shape and normals together, compares all 363 native position/normal pairs,
renders both views and repeats the balanced removal and clean exit.
Runtime fixtures cover source drift,
immutable capture, priority, restart requirements and optional loader failures.
Native Windows, other renderer game runs and Pixel hardware qualification remain
separate. See [coverage.json](coverage.json) for the full acceptance boundary and
the [native format notes](../simpsons/re/native_mesh_data.md) for source evidence.

# Authored missions

The mission service keeps a mod's objectives, prerequisites, progress, failure state and
retry points in native code. Lua and C++ use the same operations. Your gameplay logic
checks conditions through supported game APIs and advances the appropriate objective.

This service adds authored missions alongside the campaign. Original campaign game-flow
integration, general encounter hooks and mission HUD presentation remain separate
parts of the full kit. The [Mission editor](MISSION_EDITOR.md) authors route
objectives and shared prop scenes through the native menus. [Combat workshop](COMBAT.md)
combines this service with owned targets and real native death notifications;
ordinary removal does not award a defeat.

## Start with the working project

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py new "My route" --id yourname.route --author "Your name" --template mission-walk
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py validate "My route"
```

The project creates **Options → Extras → Mods → Mission example**. Load a level, then
start the mission there. Move a family member 12 units from their starting point and
bring an explorer back. Each loaded member has their own origin; an inactive member
already elsewhere, or waiting at home, cannot finish somebody else's route. The mission
has a simulation-time limit, a recorded objective retry point, failure and replay actions.
The source comments explain every part. Creation and package import leave it disabled.

The family list is not a logical controller assignment. The example uses character identity
for its small shared route and reacquires live handles for each query. More elaborate mods
need the player/entity lifecycle and assignment APIs appropriate to their roles.

## Define objectives

Register definitions during `initialize`, or recreate them during `state.loaded` when
they depend on restored mod state:

```lua
game.on("initialize", function()
    game.missions.register({
        id = "delivery", title = "Special delivery", revision = 1,
        objectives = {
            {id = "collect", title = "Collect three items", goal = 3},
            {id = "deliver", title = "Deliver the items", requires = {"collect"}}
        }
    })
end)
```

Ids are local to the mod, so two mods can both use `delivery`. Goals default to 1.
Prerequisites must refer to existing objectives and cannot form cycles. An objective
marked `optional = true` does not block mission completion. At least one objective
must be required. Put displayed text in locale catalogs for translations.

Start an idle mission from a gameplay or menu callback with `game.missions.start("delivery")`.
When your script has verified a condition, call
`game.missions.advance("delivery", "collect", 1)`. Progress clamps to the goal. Locked
objectives reject progress; completing every required objective completes the mission.
The service does not manufacture pickup, death or encounter events that the game adapter
has not implemented.

## Inspect and react

`missions.get(id)` returns a snapshot. `missions.list()` lists this mod's definitions and
progress. Mission status is `idle`, `active`, `completed` or `failed`. Objectives include
`progress`, `goal` and a state such as `locked`, `active` or `completed`.

```lua
game.on("mission.changed", function(event)
    local mission = event.mission
    game.log.info(mission.title .. ": " .. mission.status)
end)
```

Each event includes the current mission, change reason and a revision. Multiple changes
to one mission coalesce. A callback cannot recursively deliver its newly queued changes
in the same tick. Delivery rotates through a shared budget, up to 32 callbacks per tick;
the time budget is checked between callbacks. Keep callbacks short. Events belong to the
defining mod and disappear when that owner retires. Undelivered changes are saved, so a
restore does not lose a pending completion notification.

The native menu APIs can display progress and expose start/retry actions, as the example
does. Creator inspection also includes each mod's mission state. C++ plugins use
`RegisterMission`, `StartMission`, `AdvanceObjective`, `Mission` and `Missions` on `Game`.

## Failure and saves

`missions.fail(id, reason)` fails an active mission. `missions.checkpoint(id)` records its
current objective progress. `missions.restart(id)` retries from that point when one exists;
passing `false` starts from the beginning and discards the old retry point.

An objective retry point changes mission progress. It does not rewind the world. Restore
associated objects and world effects through their supported APIs, or use a game checkpoint.
The game's checkpoint/exact-save sidecars separately retain the mission service state with
the rest of the mod profile. Store your script's own coordinates, choices and counters in
`game.state`; keep live handles out of saved state.

## Code reload and migration

An unchanged objective contract restores automatically after `state.loaded`. Titles,
descriptions and display order may change. Goals, prerequisites, optional flags and revision
changes require a migration. Missing old definitions also need an explicit migration or a
fresh project session.

The callback receives this mod's saved service state as `event.missions`. Edit a copy of
that snapshot to match the new definitions, then pass it to
`game.missions.restore(event.missions)`. This operation is available only during that
preflight callback. Validate both current progress and any retry point, and keep completion
and prerequisite states consistent. An invalid migration rejects the replacement before
the old runtime is retired. New definitions absent from the old save start idle.

Ordinary save callbacks may inspect missions, but cannot register, advance, restore or
otherwise change them. Native plugins follow the same rules through the shared host API.

## Limits

A mod can register 16 missions, with 128 across the runtime. A mission has at most 32
objectives. Ids contain 1 to 80 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, underscores or hyphens.
Goals and increments must be finite and no greater than one billion. Goals are positive;
increments may be zero. Definitions fit 64 KiB. Registration reserves enough room for
progress, retry points, pending events and escaped failure text within a 256 KiB saved
service quota per mod. Oversized definitions fail before replacing an existing mission.

# Mission editor

Create a **Mission editor** project in **File → New project** in desktop Modkit, or use the same bundled template from the repository root:

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py new "My mission" --id yourname.mission --author "Your name" --template mission-editor
```

The project starts disabled. Its main.lua uses the shared Scene editor in
scene.lua; the template generator supplies that module from the Scene editor
source. Both editors use public APIs and the game's original Options movie.
They share one package, source fingerprint and saved state.

## Author and play

1. Choose **Test** and load the episode where the mission belongs. Test uses
   separate progress and keeps the normal mod profile unchanged.
2. Open **Options → Extras → Mods → Mission editor**. Add an objective at your
   character. The action uses the logical player operating the menu.
3. Choose **Reach point**, **Stay at point** or **Wait**. Move points with XYZ
   controls or stamp them at your character; set the radius or duration.
4. Choose a prerequisite and use **Add or remove prerequisite** to toggle it.
   Each new point initially follows the selected point. Cycles, missing ids
   and an entirely optional mission are rejected before replacing the draft.
5. Set optional goals, retry points, a time limit and the defeat rule. Reorder,
   duplicate and remove points as needed. Removal also removes their incoming
   prerequisite references. Undo/redo retains up to 64 edits for this session.
6. Open the project's **Scene editor** page to place props. See [Scenes](SCENES.md)
   for resource selection, transforms and ownership. This is the same editor,
   rather than another implementation with different save rules.
7. Choose **Play from beginning**. Only living family members controlled by
   logical P1/P2 satisfy visits. Staying requires the same player to remain
   continuously inside the radius; leaving or handing the visit to the other
   player resets that hold. Wait objectives need an active living player.
   Newly unlocked goals are evaluated on the next sample.
8. Use fail, retry or stop actions to revise the result. Stop before editing;
   edits replace the idle mission definition and validate the whole document.

The editor samples at roughly 0.1 simulation seconds. Pausing stops its clocks.
The timeout applies to the mission; zero disables it. The defeat rule fails
when controlled family members exist and all have fallen. An absent controller
does not count as a defeat. Optional goals do not delay completion.

A retry point records objective progress, elapsed time and continuous holds.
It does not rewind the world's enemies, props or player positions. Use a game
checkpoint or supported exact save for that. The editor stores logical player
indices, document ids and values; it does not save temporary entity handles.
Unchanged source reload and exact restore rebind the native mission service
without resetting its saved progress or partial sample clock.

## Save and share

Choose **Save mission and scene drafts**, then wait for its completion message.
The Scene editor's save action also saves both documents when used in this
project. One storage transaction writes project-drafts.json, preventing half
of a combined save from replacing the other half.

Close Test before choosing **Apply saved drafts** in Modkit. The launcher
validates both documents and checks the source fingerprint before replacing
mod.json once. If another editor changed the project, it rejects stale changed
drafts; already applied identical documents are harmless. Newer individual
drafts from older tools are also recognized. Applying drafts preserves package
metadata and creator credit.

Open **Mission settings** for titles, description, objective rules and
prerequisites. The guided form and **Edit JSON** view edit the same mod.json.
Save before testing or exporting; a conflicting source edit requires reopening
the file. Invalid graphs leave the project file untouched.

Enable **Start on episode entry** and the Scene editor's autoload toggle when
the package should start itself. The mission waits for its matching scene's
owned tags before starting. Validate and Test the applied project, then export
it. Another player imports the ZIP disabled, with its credit preserved.

## Portable document

The package's `mission` object has schema 1, a name, description, `level_root`,
positive contract `revision`, `time_limit`, `fail_on_defeat`, `auto_start` and
an `objectives` array. Each objective has an id, title, kind, position, radius,
seconds, prerequisites, optional flag and checkpoint flag. Wait rules retain a
position so changing their kind does not discard it. Positions and radii use
native float bounds; durations use simulation seconds. A document describes
one exact `.str` episode root and has at most 32 goals and 64 KiB of metadata.

`projects.document`, `projects.validate`, `projects.save` and
`projects.save_all` expose the same workflow to Lua and C++. The native mission
service separately owns progress. `missions.advance_batch` validates all
updates against the same prerequisite snapshot before committing any;
`missions.remove` retires only the caller's definition and pending changes.
See [Missions](MISSIONS.md) for service ownership and migration rules.

This route editor does not complete campaign game flow, mission HUD integration,
general enemy behavior, cinematic tracks, map/collision/navigation authoring or
device qualification. Those remain in the [full kit plan](PLAN.md).
