# Native model variants

The creator tools read the game's MMdl model definitions as named parts,
properties, states, conditions and resource references. The offline writer can
change reviewed scalar, vector, matrix and existing-reference fields while
preserving the original resource identity and layout.

The live package path currently supports **ModelPart.Model** choices between
already declared DFF references of the same native type. This is useful for
trying an existing model's alternate render parts. The separate
[static mesh tools](MESHES.md) edit supported existing vertex positions. New
topology, skeletons, animations, collision and dependencies remain part of the
[full kit](PLAN.md).

## Inspect and build

Build `modkit_streams` from the standalone tools, without rebuilding the game:

```sh
cmake -S modkit -B /path/to/modkit-build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build /path/to/modkit-build -j2 --target modkit_streams
```

Use the asset library or a deep `modkit_streams index` report to find the STR,
entry and exact resource name. Export a model from your own installed files:

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py --gamedata /path/to/gamedata model inspect gamehub/gamehub.str 23 frink_geo.meta.xml /path/to/frink.json --stream-tool /path/to/modkit-build/modkit_streams
```

Read `parts`, `fields` and `references` in the JSON. Keep the identity, source
hash and inspection fields intact. Put the intended edits in `changes`; for
the GameHub Frink definition, this selects its already declared second render
model for the first ModelPart:

```json
"changes": [
  {"field": "property:0", "value": "reference:2"}
]
```

These IDs identify records in that exact source, rather than memory addresses.
Do not reuse the ordinals for a different model. The source hash prevents that
kind of accidental cross-edit. A read-only inspection value edited outside
`changes` is rejected.

Create a credited data project, then build its edits:

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py new "My model variant" --kind data --id yourname.model-variant --author "Your name"
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py --gamedata /path/to/gamedata model build yourname.model-variant /path/to/frink.json --stream-tool /path/to/modkit-build/modkit_streams
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py validate yourname.model-variant
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py pack yourname.model-variant
```

`model build` checks the selected source resource and live edit policy before
writing `assets/model-edits.json` and adding `model_edits` to `mod.json`. Repeated
builds replace that resource's entry in the catalog. The package contains the
small edits and their source fingerprint, without copying an STR or DFF. Keep
your editable inspection document separately if you want to try more changes.

Use `run` with the current development executable and an absolute runtime path
to test with private progress, as described in the [main guide](README.md).
Restart the session after changing model assets. Code reload reports that a
restart is required and preserves the current instances. Imported packages stay
disabled and keep the creator credit through the existing Mods workflow.

## Priority and loading

Model edits follow whole-resource priority: the first requested mod wins, and
dependencies have lower priority. The package conflict report identifies
overlaps as `model:<resource-id>`. Different patches for one identity are not
silently combined. The winning document must match the resource's exact source
hash; a mismatch leaves that resource unchanged and identifies the mod in the
log.

The runtime captures and verifies catalog bytes before play. At the native
model loader it validates the chosen body and complete edit before committing
same-size bytes, then calls the original parser once. The game continues to
own binding, rendering and teardown. No file reads or replacement GPU buffers
are introduced in that callback. Model changes persist for the loaded resource;
disabling or changing an asset package requires restarting the game.

## Offline research and qualification

For a single extracted named-resource chunk, `model-inspect RESOURCE [OUTPUT]`
exports its description and `model-edit RESOURCE DOCUMENT OUTPUT` writes a new
chunk. Outputs must be new paths. Scalars and reviewed vectors/matrices are
available here for format research; their component behavior is not qualified
by the live variant policy. Unsupported types, shared data and unknown layouts
stay read-only or are rejected.

The reference fixture runs the unchanged original relocation and inverse
routines and compares every payload byte and surrounding guards. A private
installed-game check covers 2,616 definitions, including typed offline edits to
2,351 of them. This qualifies the binary reader/writer and pointer layout.
Runtime fixtures separately cover immutable source capture, source drift,
priority, restart requirements and the production hook's single-call/register/
exception behavior. A private Linux Vulkan comparison also loads the Frink
variant through the original resource binder, verifies its selected native DFF,
renders source/copy views, resumes simulation and removes the owned copy with
the original world count restored. Both runs exit cleanly. This covers that
existing-resource variant; new geometry, broader components and native
Windows/Pixel qualification remain separate. Check [coverage.json](coverage.json)
for the current acceptance boundaries.
guides.PLAN.md:
# Modkit implementation plan

The release gate is the full suite below. A working foundation or one example does not
complete the kit. `coverage.json` records the current evidence and unfinished work;
`api.json` lists implemented operations only.

The [standalone editor plan](EDITOR_PLAN.md) defines the requested professional
desktop application, real renderer viewport, asset browser, direct manipulation
and integrated help. It shares this kit's formats and services. Android keeps
mod importing and profile controls; creator tools belong in Windows/Linux Modkit.

## Creator experience and completion standard

The goal is a community that can make small changes, new missions, characters, maps and
larger conversions through approachable, documented tools. Judge completion by what a
creator can build and share. Code indexes, readable internal names and individual hooks
support that work; they do not complete the creator experience.

Use one project format throughout this workflow:

1. **Create.** The standalone Modkit offers guided projects with working, commented templates for
   gameplay, missions, assets and translations. A first visible change needs no C++ compiler
   or knowledge of generated functions. Advanced native plugins remain available.
2. **Edit.** Creators use named properties, events and Lua APIs with completion and examples.
   Artists get documented asset import/export and previews. Object, mission and cinematic
   editors use the game's native menus and save back into the same editable project.
3. **Test.** A Test action selects isolated progress and the project's test scene/checkpoint.
   Supported edits reload with useful state; changes needing a restart are identified clearly.
   Errors identify the mod, source file and affected object or resource.
4. **Validate.** Report missing dependencies, conflicting replacements, invalid assets and
   unsupported target capabilities before export. Distinguish implemented features from
   platform behavior that has actually been qualified.
5. **Share.** Export an installable package with credits, version, requirements and optional
   editable source. Another player imports it through desktop or Android Mods, sees its
   dependencies/conflicts, and can disable it while preserving vanilla files and progress.

The acceptance projects must demonstrate a complete mission with objectives, encounters,
failure/restart and checkpoints; an imported character or prop with its required resources;
an authored playable area with collision and navigation; and translated text through the
native UI. These supplement the full suite below. Tutorials must reproduce each supported
workflow from a clean creator project, without private scripts or undocumented addresses.
The save-system example is shelved. Prioritize small, practical starter projects and a
guided translation-pack workflow instead; keep existing save files and research intact.

Prioritize complete creator workflows. Finish the missing mission/lifecycle/ownership APIs
for a source-commented mission project, then qualify a complete asset import/load/retirement
path and build editors on those same public services. Reuse the current runtime, profiles,
packages, translation editor and creator bridge. Expand research names as those workflows
need them; naming every generated function is not a prerequisite for a usable modding kit.

Hit & Run's documented mod packaging, asset tools and editor assistance provide useful
workflow references: [creating mods](https://docs.donutteam.com/docs/LucasSimpsonsHitAndRunModLauncher/Mods/CreatingMods),
[tool documentation](https://github.com/donutteam/docs), and
[Lua editor definitions](https://github.com/donutteam/lucas-mod-launcher-lua).
Our STR/RenderWare tools and native adapters must implement this game's own formats and
behavior; these references do not establish file or plugin compatibility.

Current creator deliveries include the desktop [source workflow](CREATOR_WORKFLOW.md)
and the [mission service](MISSIONS.md). Android imports and manages packages. The route example proves
objectives, failure/retry, saved state and reload in a private Linux scene. It does not
complete campaign encounters, mission HUD integration or asset authoring.
The [Mission editor](MISSION_EDITOR.md) adds native route authoring with the shared
prop Scene editor, prerequisite validation, continuous visits and timed goals,
retry points, undo/redo and atomic combined drafts. The launcher offers guided
mission properties. Cinematic editing, campaign/HUD integration, complete enemy
behavior and platform qualification remain in the full gate.

The [owned-object workflow](ENTITIES.md) adds safe loaded-template registration, removal,
reload transfer and an ownership example in both creator launchers. Private Linux checks
cover two independent mods and failure cleanup. General component/transform authoring,
broader spawn-class acceptance, exact-snapshot game qualification and device runs remain
part of the gate.

Owned-object world transforms and placement now use the original frame getter
and class setter, including parent conversion and character-controller dispatch.
Full world-pose authoring now also dispatches the class matrix setter, including
rotation, scale and native model/controller notifications. The commented Owned
objects project exposes those operations in its native menu. Broader typed
components and collision-rich placement remain separate work.

Resident template discovery now reads the original definition index and native
class registry, rather than depending entirely on live source instances or a
fixed class list. Distinct behavior records stay selectable. A private Linux
hub run exposes 276 templates, including 106 without a live source object,
and qualifies retained ScriptableProp creation, world placement, simulation
and balanced removal. Original lookup comparisons, stale-owner guards,
sanitizers and Windows/Android cross-compiles cover the reader. Foreign archive
loading now has an experimental native-menu implementation. The source browser
indexes 415 installed SimG archives, requests the episode catalog and selected
archive through the original loader, holds foreign layers inactive and retains
their definitions. A Linux hub run adds 165 selectable templates from 343 foreign
definitions, without creating source actors. Native release returns 17 files to
the original 14 and the object count to 797, preserving all 844 baseline resource
bindings. An exact save restores both the source and its owned prop after their
retirement; a second release preserves those same baseline resources. The game
exits normally. Broader class behavior and native Windows/Pixel qualification
remain in the resource-streaming gate; resources are not all spawnable entities.

The retained source session now accepts up to eight archives without replacing
older spawned objects. A private Linux Vulkan run combines eight archives from
two episodes, retains 1,671 definitions, exercises native-IO cancellation and
claim rollback, and restores three independently posed props through exact saves
and code reload. Last-owner retirement returns 26 files to fourteen and 800
objects to 797, preserving all 844 baseline resource bindings and exiting zero.
The commented Library objects creator page includes retained-archive counts and
explicit cancellation; public APIs and save preflight use the same ownership
rules. Eighteen Windows x64/NoAVX2/Android ARM64 object compiles pass; live device
and broader behavior acceptance remain open.

The [Scene editor](SCENES.md) now supplies the first native prop-scene workflow:
stable owned tags, original definition identities, XYZ movement, yaw, uniform
scale, duplication, removal and bounded undo/redo in the original Options menu.
Validated drafts transfer from isolated Test storage into mod.json with source
revision checks, then export and import disabled with creator credit. Private
Linux checks exercise actual editor actions, exact/reload rebinding and fresh
imported-scene autoload, returning to all 797 objects, fourteen files and 844
baseline bindings on retirement. This does not complete map/collision,
encounter, mission or cinematic editing; native Windows/Pixel acceptance remains.
Native mod pages also refresh delayed row/title changes, preserve the current
slider selection and normalize a page offset when callbacks shorten its rows.
A private Linux keyboard/menu regression qualifies those cases, including an
actual paused source reload; unchanged pages keep their APT animations intact.

The [combat workflow](COMBAT.md) adds native health queries, scripted damage,
healing and owned death notifications. Combat workshop combines those services
with authored objectives, failure, checkpoint retry and reload rebinding. The
source project has deterministic host checks; private Linux checks separately
exercise actual loaded brawler resources. Broader enemy activation, AI,
collision/script dependencies, campaign HUD integration and device qualification
remain required before treating it as a complete campaign encounter workflow.

Owned visibility queries and hide/reveal requests now use the original native
model/scene methods. The owner contributes one balanced hide request, transferred
on reload and canceled by a native force-show. This is a visual authoring service;
AI suspension, targeting, navigation and complete enemy behaviors remain in the gate.

Loaded model GUIDs distinguish catalog variants and link them to named archive
metadata. The native loader supplies owned name strings without an additional
disk scan; ambiguous and replaced payloads do not lend stale labels. Combat
workshop includes an in-game template picker and keeps the encounter's resource
separate from the template being browsed. This is loaded-model selection, not
complete prefab/behavior authoring. Controlled Frink source/copy views now match,
including all 26 geometry/material bindings; other scripted appearances and
classes remain acceptance work.

Native camera authoring exposes applied world poses, rotation, vertical lens
angles and targeted release through the original camera writer. Its shared
Camera workshop captures and previews shots in the original menu. Ownership,
manual takeover, saved pose validation and projection arithmetic have focused
checks; full-scene exact restore, tracks, visual editing and device qualification
remain in the camera gate.

The [model tools](MODELS.md) add a typed MMdl reader and fixed-size writer,
checked against all 2,616 installed definitions and the original relocation
routines. Source-checked ModelPart variants use prepared package documents,
existing native references and the original loader's ownership. A private Linux
Frink comparison qualifies native binding, rendered source/copy views, simulation
and balanced cleanup for that variant. Broader live acceptance, new geometry/rig
import, collision, animation and dependency authoring remain in the typed-asset gate.

The [mesh attribute workflow](MESHES.md) now exports reviewed preinstanced positions
and triangles as OBJ and packages bounded position edits. All 5,533 installed
mesh resources and 20,490 native blocks pass the original relocation/copy oracle.
A private Linux Vulkan coffee-table edit verifies 363 live vertices, rendered
prop views and balanced native removal. Opt-in packed normal authoring adds
matching directions for shape edits; 1,881,360 source normals round-trip exactly
and a second edited-prop run verifies native positions and normals. New topology,
automatic normal generation, multipart native draws, skinning, collision and
platform acceptance remain in the asset gate.

Reviewed float2 UV streams support independent texture-coordinate edits on
static and skinned geometry. Byte-exact writer checks cover 6,436,832 UV pairs
across 15,321 geometries, including 12,176 skinned ones. A private Linux Frink
run verifies the bound vertex stream, preserves skinning and other attributes,
renders both views and removes the owned NPC with its world count restored.
Texture-image import, new seams/topology, rigging and multipart draws remain.

## Runtime and creator tools

| Area | Required delivery | Acceptance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public SDK | Stable C ABI, readable C++ helpers, Lua completion and generated reference | The same creator project builds independently of the game on supported targets. |
| Game code discovery | Whole-tree function inventory, direct call sites, indirect-call limits, reviewed names and source evidence | Creators can search by game system, follow the implementation and find a public API; changes invalidate stale results without renaming generated symbols. |
| Script runtime | Isolated Lua state, memory and callback budgets, simulation timers, explicit failures | Faults retire one mod and its dependents without stranding resources or affecting unrelated mods. |
| Profiles and packages | Dependencies, conflicts, ordered priority, creator credits, fingerprints, import/export | Desktop and Android install disabled, resolve the same profile, preserve base files and isolate saves. |
| Persistence | Namespaced asynchronous storage, checkpoint state and exact-save sidecars | Read-after-write, restart, failed writes, cancellation, changed-source rejection and restore preflight are qualified. |
| Code reload | Background verification, immutable code, staged initialization, state and timer migration | Lua and native code reload during play; failed preparation keeps the current instances; shutdown and cancellation remain bounded. |
| Owned resources | Per-mod and per-generation cleanup for every reversible host service | Retiring an owner preserves other owners and manual controls; saves restore complete supported host state. |
| Native UI | Original menu movies, mod pages and authoring tools, dynamic input prompts | Controller, keyboard, mouse, touch and both logical players work through the game's menus. |
| Creator automation | Local authenticated inspection, bounded named operations and repeatable projects | Tools can inspect, drive and diagnose mods without arbitrary memory writes, script evaluation or game-window guessing. |

## Game adapters and authoring

| Area | Required delivery | Acceptance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Players and entities | Named queries, lifecycle events, transforms, components and owned spawns | Handles expire safely on unload, deletion, reload and restore; spawned objects clean up through proven game routines. |
| Combat and AI | Health, damage, abilities, targeting, behavior and encounter extension points | A creator acceptance mod changes a complete encounter with correct co-op, save and unload behavior. |
| Missions and progression | Objectives, events, ScoreKeeper, unlocks, checkpoints and game flow | A source-commented mission project can start, complete, fail, restart and restore without hardcoded recomp addresses. |
| Cameras and cinematics | Complete camera state, tracks, sequencing and cutscene hooks | Playback, cancellation, checkpoints, exact restore and returning to the gameplay camera are qualified. |
| Visual editors | In-game layout, object, mission and cinematic editing | Editable projects round-trip through the public kit and stay in the game's original UI. |
| Debug library | Categorized whole-game catalog, search, paging and source identities | All installed resources are indexed; actual cross-level use follows verified dependencies and initialization. |
| Resource streaming | Dependency-aware cross-level loading, spawning and retirement | A resource from another level loads, behaves correctly, releases safely and restores from a save. |

## Assets and translations

| Area | Required delivery | Acceptance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Container tools | Lossless STR/RefPack inspection, rebuilds, merged catalog corrections and provenance | Native decoder comparisons, changed sizes, compression, catalog/dependency layout changes and native loader projects agree. |
| Typed assets | Meshes, rigs, animations, collision, navigation and worlds | Each type has documented bounds, a supported writer and a native loader round-trip acceptance project. |
| Presentation extensions | Audio, textures, materials and renderer extensions | Projects work across supported renderers and platforms with explicit ownership, save and unload behavior. |
| Translation workflow | Searchable source catalogs, editor, validation, progress, partial language packs and translator credit | Placeholders and dynamic button tags survive; stale sources are detected; the native text lookup displays translations. |
| Fonts and layout | Font import, Unicode coverage, right-to-left text and text fitting | Acceptance languages render correctly in menus, gameplay and cutscenes on desktop and Android. |

## Bundled example and delivery

Bundle commented starter projects for native menus, logical-player actions, simulation
timers, scenes, missions and the supported asset workflows. Each project starts disabled,
uses named public APIs and includes editable locale catalogs. A translator can create a
partial language pack from the installed game or another mod through the desktop editor,
validate it and export a credited ZIP for desktop and Android. The original slot menus
remain active while the separate save-library experiment is shelved.

Qualification covers Linux, Steam Deck desktop and Gaming Mode, native Windows and Pixel
hardware. Cross-compilation and Proton checks are useful evidence and are recorded separately
from native Windows and Android device runs. Creator projects must cover the systems above,
dependency failures, overlapping mods, bad packages, slow storage, hot reload, co-op, level
changes, checkpoints, exact restore and shutdown.

Finish and document these checks before staging the full kit, migrating the save example,
or delivering a release package as complete. Preserve existing source work, installed builds,
real saves and the workspace's 25 GiB free-space reserve throughout development.
guides.README.md:
# Simpsons Modkit

The goal is a complete creator workflow for gameplay mods, missions, characters, maps,
assets and translations: create a project, edit it, test it and share it through the
desktop Modkit application. The [creator experience standard](PLAN.md#creator-experience-and-completion-standard)
defines that delivery; parts of it are still under development.

The modkit gives mods named game operations instead of recompiled function addresses.
C++ plugins and Lua scripts use the same game-thread adapters. Mod settings pages use
the original Options movie, including its controller, keyboard, mouse and touch input.

The [loaded-object guide](ENTITIES.md) covers mod-owned spawns, world transforms,
placement, removal, reload transfer and the **Owned objects** creator project
shared by the desktop editor and CLI.
The [Scene editor](SCENES.md) adds an in-game prop authoring project with
placement, rotation, scale, undo/redo and portable scene drafts. Apply a tested
draft in Modkit, then export it with your creator credit.
The [Mission editor](MISSION_EDITOR.md) adds reach, continuous stay and wait
objectives, prerequisites, retry points and simulation-time rules. Its shared
Scene editor saves both documents together; the desktop Inspector also offers a guided
mission form for names and rules.
Owned objects also have native visibility queries and idempotent hide/reveal
requests, preserving authored hide requests and transferring across code reload.

This is development work. The full suite is a release requirement. New level and character
asset authoring, AI/combat extension points, the remaining visual editors and complete platform
qualification are still being implemented. The API catalog lists implemented operations;
it does not advertise those unfinished systems. The [implementation plan](PLAN.md) keeps the
full release scope and acceptance requirements together.

## Start a mod

Open the separate desktop **Modkit** application and choose **File → New project**. Choose a commented gameplay,
mission or file-replacement project, enter your creator credit, then use the source
editor, Validate, Test and Export ZIP. Test keeps separate progress and leaves the normal
profile unchanged. The [workspace guide](EDITOR_WORKFLOW.md) covers the native editor, viewport, assets and built-in help. Android imports/manages packages; authoring stays on Windows/Linux.

The same templates are available from the repository root:

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py new "Health tools" --id yourname.health-tools --author "Your name"
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py validate yourname.health-tools
```

The Lua example registers a native menu in **Options → Extras → Mods**. It refills health,
changes damage protection and enables the free camera through the existing game code.
Game operations are available from registered callbacks. See `api.json` and the generated
reference for names and arguments.

```lua
game.on("level.ready", function()
    for _, player in ipairs(game.players.list()) do
        game.log.info(player.character)
    end
end)
```

For C++, create a project with `--kind native`, then run `build <id>`. CMake builds the plugin
against the public SDK without compiling the game. `--cmake-arg` passes compiler/toolchain
settings and `--target` selects `windows-x64`, `linux-x64` or `android-arm64`. A package needs
a matching native binary on each platform where it runs. Lua projects use the same source
across platforms.

## Author a mission

Use `new "My route" --template mission-walk --id yourname.route --author "Your name"`
for a commented mission with native menu controls, objective dependencies, failure, retry
points and saved progress. It uses player-position queries and simulation time. The
[mission guide](MISSIONS.md) describes Lua/C++ operations, ownership, saves and reload migrations.
The [combat guide](COMBAT.md) adds original damage/healing operations and owned
native death events. `--template combat-workshop` creates a commented encounter
workshop with targets, objectives, visibility controls, failure, retry and reload rebinding. Campaign
integration, mission HUD work and broader AI authoring remain in the full plan.

## Find the game code behind a feature

The creator CLI shares the existing codegraph index. It scans generated functions and
links their callers, hand-written adapters, reverse-engineering notes and reviewed
descriptive names. No game window, installed game data or compiler is needed.

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py code build
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py code search health
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py code show ScoreKeeper.GetScore
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py code callers ScoreKeeper.GetScore
```

Use the linked public operations when writing a mod. A research name describes an internal
function; it does not provide a safe public calling signature. The address symbols stay
intact through regeneration. See [code navigation](CODE_NAVIGATION.md) for source checks,
adding reviewed names and extending the public APIs.

## Install and test

`pack <id>` produces a ZIP with a SHA-256 file inventory. `install <zip>` validates and
extracts it into a new folder, disabled. `enable <id>` checks dependencies and conflicts.
The first requested mod has the highest file priority; dependencies initialize first and
have lower asset priority than their dependents. The runtime merges file lookup and directory
enumeration, including added files. Original game files are not overwritten.

Use `run <id> --exe /absolute/path/to/simpsons --lib-dir /absolute/path/to/runtime` for an
isolated test. It creates separate userdata and prints its location. A test run never uses
your real saves. `--gamedata` selects your own installed game files.

The launcher also imports packages and changes the active profile while the game is closed.
Older game builds cannot enable mods; a build with the mod runtime supplies
`simpsons-modkit.json`. Android uses the same Mods tab, with a system ZIP picker,
background installation, notifications, progress and cancellation. Device qualification is
still pending.

## Translations

Translators can use the local editor without writing Lua or C++. It has a source column,
translation column, search across every table, untranslated filter and progress count. It saves UTF-8 JSON in
the project's `.translations` folder. Keep that folder with the project's source; working
catalogs are excluded from installed ZIPs.

To translate a mod that supplies a source catalog:

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py translate new "French health tools" --of yourname.health-tools --locale fr --author "Your name"
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py translate edit "French health tools"
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py translate check "French health tools"
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py translate build "French health tools"
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py pack "French health tools"
```

The resulting language pack depends on the original mod and credits its translator. Install
it through the normal desktop or Android Mods tab. **Mod text language** follows the game's
language unless a code such as `fr` or `pt-BR` is entered. Missing regional translations fall
back to the parent language, then the mod's source language. Missing keys show their key.

Mod authors put text in `locales/en.json`, declare it in `mod.json`, and use stable keys:

```json
{
  "default_locale": "en",
  "locales": {"en": "locales/en.json", "fr": "locales/fr.json"}
}
```

The catalog is a flat JSON object, for example `{"health.refill": "Refill health"}`.
Use `game.locale.text("health.refill")` in Lua or `game.Text("health.refill")` in C++.
Named values work as `game.locale.text("welcome", {name = "Lisa"})` for `"Hello {name}"`.
Catalogs load before callbacks, so looking up text does not read from disk during a frame.

Game text uses the same editor. Build the creator tools once, then pass their executable:

```sh
cmake -S modkit -B /path/to/modkit-build
cmake --build /path/to/modkit-build -j2 --target modkit_streams
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py translate --stream-tool /path/to/modkit-build/modkit_streams new "My game translation" --locale fr --author "Your name"
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py translate edit "My game translation"
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py translate check "My game translation"
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py translate --stream-tool /path/to/modkit-build/modkit_streams build "My game translation"
```

The exporter reads your installed archives, including embedded dialogue and in-game cutscene
text. Identical tables are edited once. Building emits a small `locales/game-text.json` catalog;
the game applies it through the original text lookup. Game archives and dialogue identifiers
remain intact. Once a project contains its source identities, building it needs neither the
stream tool nor the original game files. The stream tool is needed for the initial export.
Use the pack's base game language (English by default) when playing it. Embedded table export
currently targets English game data; `--base` selects other named global tables in your copy.

Each table is matched by its original content hash after normalizing runtime pointers.
Each translated line also checks the source string. Unmatched content keeps its original text.
Translation strings are allocated before play and retained with native resources; lookups
perform no filesystem I/O. `text.lookup` reads a loaded game text ID for inspection or a mod
that needs the game's text. It reports `found=false` for unloaded tables.

Button tags (`[RDDown]`), numbered values (`%1`), printf placeholders and named values must
survive translation. Check reports missing or changed tags before a build. Narrow game
tables use Windows-1252; characters needing a different font are reported, never silently
changed to question marks. Unicode font import, right-to-left layout and complete font
coverage remain part of the unfinished asset suite.

## Asset library

The debug menu's **Game-wide library**, also available from Spawner → Entire game, indexes
all installed episodes and enabled mod files. It groups characters, models, animations,
effects, textures, worlds, physics, audio, text, movies and other resources. Named object
definitions link to their models, character banks and mesh parts before spawning. A worker starts
when the library is first requested. Search, initial-letter filters, paging and source
locations help inspect large categories without building thousands of menu rows per frame.

`assets.search` exposes the same bounded queries to creator scripts. Check `ready` while
indexing. Friendly names retain their original artist names and source paths in the details.
Open a linked object and choose **Load and spawn** to use its original source data.
Resource identities describe archive content; they are not live entity handles.
The spawner uses validated live objects and retained definitions from fully loaded native
streams. Destroying the original object need not remove its template. It keeps distinct
behavior records separate and discovers additional placeable classes through the native
registry; extra categories appear automatically. **Spawner → Objects from other levels**
is an experimental native source loader: choose an episode archive, wait for its catalog
and dependencies, then use the regular spawner categories. Up to eight archives can stay
loaded in one retained session. Additions are serialized and preserve earlier objects;
a failed or canceled addition removes only its new native files. Mods share the session
through `assets.load_source` and `assets.source_status`; `assets.source_streams` lists its
accepted archives, and `assets.templates` supplies current spawn handles once ready.
Spawning from a retained source automatically acquires a lease for the spawning mod.
`assets.cancel_source` withdraws a pending addition while preserving an earlier lease.
The commented **Library objects** creator project demonstrates this path. Require its
new operations in your manifest so older hosts reject unsupported projects clearly.
Each owner releases only its lease; all accepted archives and dependencies stay together
until the last release. The original loader then removes their copies and files while
preserving other level files, including later streamed files. Exact saves retain every
archive's load identities and validate mod claims before restoring guest memory. Legacy
single-source exact saves remain readable.
This does not establish scene-specific AI or boss behavior for every class;
see [object ownership](ENTITIES.md).

Owned objects also have full world-pose authoring through
`entities.set_transform`: position, orientation and scale use the original
class matrix setter, including cached scale and model/controller notifications.
The **Owned objects** example includes native menu actions for moving, rotating,
growing and shrinking a prop. See [transforms](ENTITIES.md#transforms) for parent
conversion, supported inputs and collision/script limits.

An optional native reference check validates compression against the game's own generated
decoder, with no game window or graphics backend:

```sh
cmake -S modkit -B /path/to/modkit-build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DSIMPSONS_MODKIT_REFERENCE_CHECKS=ON
cmake --build /path/to/modkit-build -j2 --target modkit_refpack_check
/path/to/modkit-build/modkit_refpack_check --self-test /path/to/self-test.json
/path/to/modkit-build/modkit_refpack_check /path/to/gamedata /path/to/game-streams.json
```

A single STR file can be supplied instead of the game folder. Each compressed entry is
decoded with both implementations, re-encoded, and checked again through the original
whole-buffer and asynchronous game routines. The step checks compare output, cursor
updates, command boundaries, return values, saved registers and untouched memory. Zero-byte,
small, block-sized and live-loader requests are included. Corrupt-input fixtures also check
that a rejected native step restores its buffers and registers before falling back.
Reports include the reference source identities, entry counts, compared bytes and timings.
Those timings exclude guest heap checks and do not measure frame rate.
Re-encoding uses bounded reference matching and calculates the input headroom required
for decoding in place. It also reports the original and re-encoded storage sizes.
The tool uses temporary memory, reads the source files and writes the chosen JSON report.
Add `--decode-only` after the report path to compare installed streams without running
the encoder. Keep the complete check for qualifying an encoder or changed resource writer.

Rebuilt STR files can need larger buffers even when their decoded content is unchanged.
The game's StreamTOC catalogs reserve those buffers before reading a child archive's header.
The merged mod filesystem checks the winning STR headers at startup and corrects the
catalog's allocation and pool fields on reads. This also accounts for overlapping mods;
original archives and installed packages stay untouched. Missing catalog dependencies,
changed entry counts, unknown pools and allocations beyond the catalog format fail before
the game starts. Changed compressed catalogs need a separate rebuilder.

Inspect those corrections without starting the game:

```sh
/path/to/modkit-build/modkit_streams catalogs /path/to/gamedata /path/to/catalog-report.json --overlay /path/to/your-mod/gamedata
```

Additional `--overlay` folders use highest-to-lowest priority. Private Linux runs qualify
recompressed global text and a resized LH2 edit through the native loader. This does not
qualify arbitrary meshes, dependencies or every edited resource type. Those typed asset
pipelines remain under development.

The [model tools](MODELS.md) export native MMdl definitions as readable parts,
properties, states and references. They build source-checked ModelPart variants
into small credited packages, preserving original resource ownership and the
existing dependency set. The [mesh attribute tools](MESHES.md) export supported
geometry as OBJ and package bounded vertex, normal and UV edits through the
native loader. Reviewed character UV streams can change while their skinning,
positions and normals stay intact. Topology, materials and resource ownership
are preserved. New topology,
rig import and live device qualification remain in the full kit gate.

## Lifetimes and saves

Game handles are temporary identities, not addresses. Reacquire them after a level unload or
save restore. `players.list` currently enumerates loaded family entities; its `slot` is a list
index, not a controller assignment. `input.players` describes actual input assignments.

## Reading controls

`game.input.state(0)` and `game.input.state(1)` read the controls the game received for
P1 and P2. Keyboard, gamepad and touch inputs follow the existing player assignments.
Each mod sees the same snapshot for a modkit frame; reads do not poll devices or consume
mouse movement. Use `pressed` for a single action and `buttons` for a held control:

```lua
game.on("simulation", function()
    local input = game.input.state(0)
    if input.sampled and input.available and input.pressed.x then
        -- Run your P1 action once for this press.
    end
end)
```

Face names are logical controls, regardless of the glyphs on a particular controller.
Sticks range from -1 to 1 with positive Y upwards; analog triggers range from 0 to 1.
Trigger button flags become held above 30/255. A quick tap between updates can set both
`pressed` and `released`. First samples, reconnects and restored timelines establish a
baseline without inventing presses. A failed poll releases the old held controls.

`sampled` says the game has polled that port since the last reset. `updated` says a poll
arrived this frame. `available` is that poll's result, rather than a physical hotplug
query: a port the game is not polling retains its last values and clears its old edges.
Snapshots may reflect the preceding game poll. Read gameplay actions in `simulation`;
use `ui.action` for native menus. Never store transient input or edges in saved state.

`input.players` also reports device identity, name and kind. Its existing `prompts` field
keeps the configured override, such as `auto`; `prompt_family` resolves that override
to Xbox, PlayStation, Nintendo, Steam Deck or keyboard. These records do not associate
a loaded family entity with a controller. Use `players.controlled(0)` or
`players.controlled(1)` for the currently bound family character, or inspect
`input_player` in `players.list()`. AI, unbound and ambiguous actors have no input
owner. Requery during simulation when characters switch or co-op players join/drop
out; the old handle may remain a valid AI actor. A paused or temporarily blocked
input does not remove its assignment. C++ mods use `Game::ControlledPlayer(player)`,
`Game::Input(player)` and `Game::InputPlayers()`. The generated Lua reference includes
typed player records, snapshot fields and
editor completion. See the [Input observer](examples/input-observer/main.lua) template
for a commented P1/P2 reader and native Options page. New launcher projects stay disabled.

The game adapter observes `sub_82B766A8`, the original XInputGetState wrapper, after its
single original call and the existing camera/menu filters. A scope in the existing
input hook covers its early returns. An offline check compares every guest register and
memory byte with the unchanged reader and equivalent final filters, including failed/null
reads, synthesized menu input, both ports, exception unwinding and resets during a poll.
The ownership reader uses the character's human-control marker and actual input
binding, independently of family order and viewport. Its fixture compares those
reads with the original human-control and button-dispatch routines. These shared
host services are independent of the rendering backend; compilation
and live platform qualification are recorded separately in `coverage.json`.

## Persistent mod state

Store persistent Lua values in `game.state`. State must be JSON-compatible: string keys,
finite numbers, booleans, strings and contiguous arrays. Functions, game handles, threads and
userdata do not belong in saved state. Do not keep a local reference to the state table across
restores; read `game.state` inside callbacks.

`save_mode` is `state`, `stateless` or `checkpoint`. Stateful native mods supply both serializer
callbacks and keep instance data in their plugin context. Initialization must register services
and menus without changing gameplay. Restore preflight recreates mod instances, initializes
their menus, and loads state before the game memory changes. Gameplay changes belong in
`level.ready`, `simulation`, `ui.action` or `save.restored` callbacks.

Exact saves require an identical ordered mod profile and content fingerprints. Preflight
failure keeps the running mod instances. Checkpoints and autosaves store mod state alongside
the game's slot files; checkpoint-only mods produce checkpoint saves. `save.restored` includes
`kind` (`exact` or `checkpoint`). Reacquire level objects in `level.ready` after a checkpoint.

Source verification runs on workers for both checkpoint and exact loads. Checkpoint
preparation captures its mod sidecar with the verified code, then initializes callbacks
on the game thread before replacing the working slot. Loading an older vanilla checkpoint
without a sidecar initializes fresh mod state. Invalid JSON, mismatched profiles and changed
source reject the load before working-slot replacement, keeping the running mods intact. The native
save menu keeps the load error visible when it reopens. Large-profile callback staging still
needs a separate frame budget; background file verification does not complete that work.

Damage protection and camera requests belong to the calling mod and runtime generation.
The latest active request wins. If it retires, the preceding owner's request becomes active;
when the last owner retires, the original manual value returns. Manual controls supersede
older mod requests, including a manual request for the same value. A failed mod loses its
pages, timers and requests without retiring another mod. Saved ownership includes request
order and baseline values, including authored poses and captured manual camera views.
The [camera guide](CAMERAS.md) covers pose/lens editing and the shared native-menu
Camera workshop. Checkpoints discard old-world camera requests; full-scene exact
camera restoration and cinematic tracks still need qualification.

Desktop and Android launchers give each ordered mod combination its own progress folder.
The first launch copies vanilla checkpoint progress into that folder; snapshots are not copied.
Disabling all mods returns to vanilla progress. Changing mod code or priority selects a separate
playthrough. These save paths are still under live qualification; this development kit is not
release ready.

## Script environment

Lua 5.4.9 is compiled into the game. Each mod has its own state, a 32 MiB allocation limit,
and bounded callbacks. Standard table, string, math and UTF-8 functions are available.
`require("helpers.combat")` loads this mod's `helpers/combat.lua` during initialization.
Register handlers with `game.on`; supported events are listed in the generated completion file.
Lua entrypoints and modules are verified and copied into an immutable source set before the
first game-thread callback. `require` reads that memory, not a file during play. Source is
limited to 32 MiB per mod, with at most 4 MiB in one file. Edits on disk take effect on a new
launch; exact/checkpoint restore still checks the source fingerprint before accepting it.

File/process/debug libraries, dynamic Lua loading, `__gc` finalizers and nested protected calls
are not exposed. Lua disables instruction hooks in finalizers, so they cannot meet callback limits.
The host owns protected entrypoints so script errors and budget interrupts can end a callback.
Use `game.system.try_call("world.spawn", {template = id, position = p})` for an
expected host rejection. It returns `{ok = true, value = ...}` or
`{ok = false, code = ..., error = ...}` while preserving the target's argument,
ownership, save and preflight rules. It cannot run a script function or catch a
callback timeout. C++ plugins can use `Game::TryCall` or catch `Error` from `Call`.

Persistent JSON storage is namespaced by mod ID. It is loaded before callbacks, read from memory,
and written atomically by a background worker. Reads see a queued write immediately. Check
`storage.status()` for pending writes and disk errors; shutdown drains accepted writes. Limits
are 1 MiB per file, 256 files and 16 MiB per mod, and 64 MiB across active mods. Store settings
here; put playthrough progress in `game.state` so loading a save restores it too.

Native plugins execute as native code in the game process and must catch their own exceptions
before returning through the C ABI. Their shutdown callback must finish their own threads and
release resources before returning. Save callbacks may inspect state but cannot change gameplay,
storage, pages or timers. Native images are limited to 64 MiB per library and 256 MiB per mod.

## Timers and creator inspection

Use simulation timers for cooldowns and scripted sequences rather than counting display
frames or reading a wall clock. Pausing stops them; changing the display frame rate does not
speed them up. Each mod owns its timer ids. Reusing an id replaces its pending event.

```lua
game.on("initialize", function()
    game.timers.schedule("reminder", 5, 0, {message = "Ready"})
end)

game.on("timer", function(event)
    if event.id == "reminder" then game.log.info(event.data.message) end
end)
```

An optional positive interval repeats a timer. A slow frame delivers one event and reports
the number of skipped intervals; it does not run a catch-up loop. Dispatch has a shared frame
budget and rotates through overdue timers. Timers keep their remaining delay and JSON data
in exact saves and checkpoints. `timers.cancel(id)` removes a timer; `timers.list()` inspects
this mod's pending work. Limits are 64 timers per mod, 1024 overall, 64 KiB of data per timer,
and delays up to a day. Native plugins use `Game::ScheduleTimer` and `Game::CancelTimer`.

`run --developer` enables the local creator bridge in an isolated test. The game log prints
its `session.json` path. Ordinary play does not create a session or poll for requests.
Use that path while the game runs:

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py dev --session /path/to/session.json status
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py dev --session /path/to/session.json call players.list
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py dev --session /path/to/session.json state yourname.health-tools
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py dev --session /path/to/session.json menu yourname.health-tools:tools heal --player 1
```

Status includes menu row identities, creator credits, callback cost, storage errors, pending
timers, owned host resources and a bounded lifecycle/event log. `call` accepts `--arguments` as a JSON object; game
mutations and namespaced operations require `--owner` with an active mod id. Menu activation
uses the same validation and logical-player attribution as actual input. `wait` waits for a
loaded level; `--timeout` accepts up to 30 seconds. `status --after N` filters the event log.

Use `source` for object loading without constructing a JSON call:

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py dev --session /path/to/session.json --timeout 30 source load brt/brt/challenge_mode/challenge_mode_design.str --owner yourname.library-objects --wait
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py dev --session /path/to/session.json source status --owner yourname.library-objects
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py dev --session /path/to/session.json --timeout 30 source wait --owner yourname.library-objects
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py dev --session /path/to/session.json source cancel --owner yourname.library-objects
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py dev --session /path/to/session.json source release --owner yourname.library-objects
```

Use a source path from `assets.templates` and the active mod's actual ID. `load`
requests once; `--wait` prints native file progress to stderr and leaves the final
JSON result on stdout. A timed-out wait leaves accepted loading in progress;
inspect or resume waiting instead of submitting another load. `release` returns
whether that mod released a claim and its current source status. Native cleanup
is asynchronous, and other owners can keep the group loaded.

The worker handles file I/O; the game thread executes named operations. Requests are bounded,
authenticated to one local session and expire if the game cannot service them. A repeated
request id never repeats an action. The CLI does not retry mutations after a timeout. Session
credentials remain in the private userdata folder, and the descriptor is retired at shutdown.
The bridge does not expose arbitrary Lua evaluation, game memory writes or a network listener.

### Reload code

In a creator session, edit Lua source or rebuild a native plugin, then run:

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py dev --session /path/to/session.json reload
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py dev --session /path/to/session.json reload --cancel
```

File hashes and code copies are prepared on a worker while the game continues. The game
thread initializes replacement instances and loads their JSON state before retiring the
running code. Invalid code or staged initialization that changes gameplay fails preflight
and leaves the running instances in place. Native plugins load verified private images so
their source DLL can be rebuilt on Windows while the original instance is running.

Reload preserves remaining timer delays and owned host requests. `code.reloaded` runs after
commit, with `level_ready` and a new runtime epoch. Reacquire temporary game handles there
and refresh menu values loaded from `game.state`. A failed mod can recover its JSON state
when serialization succeeded before retirement; the host refuses to silently discard state
it could not capture. Native plugins must keep instance state in their context and shut down
their own workers before returning from their shutdown callback.

Use `state.loaded` to validate saved fields, add new defaults or migrate your state schema
before commit. Its `kind` is `reload`, `exact` or `checkpoint`. This callback can update
`game.state`, staged menus and this instance's timers; it cannot change gameplay or persistent
storage. An error rejects the replacement while the old state and pages remain active.

Reload covers code in the current ordered profile. Changed metadata, dependencies, translations
or game data require a restart so loaded native resources stay consistent. Installed packages
with checksum inventories must still pass those checks; edit a creator project for development.
Status reports preparation progress and the last result. A CLI timeout leaves an accepted job
visible in status; it never retries the reload automatically. Full resource remounting and
dependency-aware streaming remain separate work.

Exact-save reads and the native checkpoint load flow verify source files in background
workers, then use immutable prepared code during game-thread preflight. Checkpoint sidecars
are also captured by the worker. Cancellation and failed preflight preserve the current mod
instances; the working slot changes only after the required preparation succeeds.

The save-library experiment is shelved. The original game save menus remain active and
existing library files are preserved. Start with the commented Script starter, Player
actions or Timed events projects instead. See [getting started](GETTING_STARTED.md) and
[language packs](TRANSLATIONS.md) for complete creation and export steps.

## Development checks

```sh
cmake -S modkit -B /path/to/modkit-build -DSIMPSONS_MODKIT_TESTS=ON
cmake --build /path/to/modkit-build -j2
ctest --test-dir /path/to/modkit-build --output-on-failure
python3 modkit/tests/test_packages.py
python3 modkit/tests/test_translations.py
python3 modkit/tests/test_developer.py
```

Set `MODKIT_CHECK_EXE` to the built `modkit_check` when running the Python checks to compare
content fingerprints across both implementations. Tests use synthetic content and private
temporary folders. Live renderer and device checks are recorded separately.

`tools/modkit/generate_api.py --output <directory>` generates the embedded API catalog,
Lua completion and Markdown reference from the same definitions.

Lua's copyright and MIT license are retained under `thirdparty/lua`. The JSON and SHA-256
implementations use the existing SDK dependencies and retain their respective licenses.

# Build a prop scene in game

**Scene editor** is a commented creator project shared by the desktop launcher,
Android launcher and CLI. Its controls use the game's original **Options →
Extras → Mods → Scene editor** menu. It places original props, edits their world
poses and saves a portable scene in your project.

This is the first scene-authoring workflow. New maps, collision meshes,
navigation, enemy encounters and mission or cinematic editors remain in the
[full implementation plan](PLAN.md).

## Create, test and share

1. In **File → New project** in Modkit, choose **Scene editor**. Enter a name, stable mod id
   and your creator credit. The new project starts disabled.
2. Choose **Test**, load a level in that isolated playthrough and open the
   editor through the game's Options menu.
3. Choose **Refresh loaded props**, select a **Prop** and use **Place
   beside my character**. Template pages contain up to forty choices. The first
   placed prop selects the scene's episode.
4. Select an authored **Object**. Change its X, Y and Z position, choose a
   movement step, rotate left/right or grow/shrink it. You can bring it beside
   your character, duplicate it or remove it. Undo and redo keep up to 64 edits
   during the current editor session. Use **More settings** to reach the next
   page of controls. Long labels are shortened for the TV menu; full object
   names stay in the document and full status messages appear in the game log.
5. Enable **Load automatically in this episode** if players should see the
   scene when they enter its episode. Choose **Save scene draft** and wait for
   the saved confirmation.
6. Close the Test game. In the launcher, choose **Apply scene draft**. Review
   the scene in mod.json, then **Validate**, **Test** and **Export ZIP**.
7. Another player imports the ZIP through the normal Mods tab. It starts
   disabled and retains your creator credit. The package contains scene
   descriptions and your script; it does not need copies of the original
   archives that supply those props.

For the CLI, create the same project with:

```sh
python3 tools/modkit/modkit.py new "My prop scene" --template scene-editor --id yourname.scene --author "Your name"
```

**Unload preview** removes this scene's owned copies and releases its resource
claim without deleting the authored document. **Load scene preview** recreates
missing copies from the original definitions. **Cancel scene loading** rolls
back copies created by that load attempt. Other mods' objects stay owned by
their creators. **Start a new empty scene** clears this scene's preview and
document; saving and applying it replaces the previous draft.

## Documents and object identity

One project has one scene, stored in the optional `scene` field of mod.json.
The schema allows up to 64 objects in one episode and a canonical document of
at most 128 KiB. A saved draft also records the exact source-project
fingerprint. Applying a draft refuses changed source, symbolic links and
malformed documents before replacing mod.json. Your name, description, credit
and other manifest fields are preserved. Re-test after editing project files
to produce a draft for their new revision.

Each object records a stable id, a display name, its original definition GUID,
native class, archive path, placement radius and full world pose. The pose has
`position`, `right`, `up` and `forward` vectors. The menu currently exposes XYZ
movement, yaw in 15-degree steps and uniform size changes of ten percent;
scripts can author other valid rotation and scale matrices.

The document never records guest pointers or temporary entity/template
handles. Stable tags are unique within their owning mod. The runtime rejects
duplicate live or pending tags before creating another object. Tags allow the
editor to recover fresh handles after code reload and exact-save restoration.
The example uses `save_mode = "state"` so its validated document participates
in both checkpoint and exact saves.

Relevant public operations are:

| Operation | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `scenes.document()` | Read the scene and source fingerprint prepared before callbacks. |
| `scenes.validate(document)` | Validate and canonicalize a document without changing the world. |
| `scenes.save(document)` | Queue a draft in the mod's namespaced storage. Check storage status for completion. |
| `world.spawn(..., tag)` | Create a supported owned object with a stable tag. |
| `world.tagged(tag)` | Get this mod's current live handle, or no handle. |
| `world.catalog()` | Discover available definition GUIDs, classes and source streams. |
| `world.status()` | Check level readiness, its episode catalog and active native streaming. |

Lua completion, the generated API reference and C++ helpers describe the full
signatures. The [loaded-object guide](ENTITIES.md) explains transform and
ownership rules; the Library objects project demonstrates selecting foreign
archives explicitly.

## Resource loading and limits

The editor matches the saved GUID and class against the native definition
catalog. If the source is missing, it requests the saved archive through the
original loader and waits for its dependencies. It never substitutes a
similarly named model. Autoload runs only when the loaded episode matches the
document. A missing or ambiguous episode catalog leaves the preview unloaded
with an explanation.

The retained source session supports up to eight selected foreign archives;
dependencies can share files. Sources stay retained while an owner needs
them. Retiring the last owner checks native file identity before releasing
owned files. The editor waits through active native streaming and handles
recoverable busy responses without discarding its pending load.

The initial template picker contains supported props. Factory availability
alone does not establish an NPC's AI, scripts, encounter activation or
navigation requirements. Moving or resizing a renderable prop also does not
author new collision geometry. These limits apply even if a model appears in
the asset library.

## Qualification

A private Linux Vulkan run exercises the public Lua editor actions, world
poses, undo/redo, tag isolation, duplicate rejection, asynchronous drafts,
exact restoration after actual source retirement and code reload. A second
fresh run loads the exported/imported scene without its original test data or
a provider mod. Removing its two copies returns the world to 797 objects,
fourteen files and all 844 baseline resource bindings, followed by a normal
exit.

Host checks cover document policy, pending/live tag uniqueness, stale drafts,
source preservation and credited disabled import. Changed C++ sources compile
for Windows x64, Windows NoAVX2 and Android ARM64; the changed Android creator
class compiles against API 36. Native Windows and Pixel interaction, storage
providers and the wider class library still need their own acceptance runs.

# Make a language pack

Open the desktop **Modkit**, then **File → New language pack**. Choose the game
or an installed mod, enter the target language code (`fr`, `pt-BR`, `es-MX`,
for example), your translator credit and a pack name. Game text is read from
your own installed files with the bundled `modkit_streams` tool. A mod needs a
`default_locale` and a source catalog; all of the small starter projects include
both.

The translation workspace lists the catalogs and shows original text beside
your translation. Search the current table, filter untranslated entries and
watch the translated/remaining counts. **Keep the original text** leaves that
entry out of your pack. Uncheck it to write a translation, including multiple
lines. **Insert tag** copies a button tag or placeholder exactly.

Use **Save table** to keep a draft. Source text and text IDs stay intact;
another editor's changed revision cannot be overwritten silently. Drafts may
contain unfinished tags. **Check pack** reports missing or changed placeholders
and font limitations, and export requires those errors to be resolved.

**Export language pack** builds and exports the installable ZIP in one step.
It includes your translations and credit, with the required mod dependency
when translating another mod. It does not include the original game archives
or your `.translations` working catalogs. Partial packs are supported: missing
entries fall back to the original text.

Keep the entire project, including `.translations`, to continue later. Select
the project and choose **File → Edit translations** to reopen it. Share the ZIP
with players; they import it in **Mods** on desktop or Android and select the
matching language. A game pack replaces the installed source language chosen
when creating it, so use that source language in the game's own settings.

The current font checks protect characters that the installed font cannot
display. A language needing additional glyphs or right-to-left layout also
needs a supported font/layout import; the editor will not silently replace
those characters with question marks.

The existing `modkit translate new/edit/check/build` commands use the same
catalogs and validation. Advanced users can keep using those commands or the
browser editor without converting projects.
